children: A sizable minority of Americans say fears over Social Security's finances will prompt them to claim early, even though doing so will reduce their monthly benefit for life.

Some 45% of Americans plan to file for Social Security benefits before 67, the age when people born in 1960 or later are entitled to their full benefit, according to the Schroders 2026 US Retirement Survey released Thursday. Just 10% plan to wait until age 70 for their maximum benefit. Of those who planned to claim before 70, four in 10 cited concerns that Social Security may run out of money or stop making payments.

Social Security has big problems, but it isn't running out of money. Instead, it's running short of what it needs to pay promised benefits. If Congress doesn't act by late 2032, the retirement trust fund will run dry and beneficiaries will face an automatic benefit cut of 22%, according to the latest projections. Incoming payroll taxes and other program income will continue to fund the remaining 78%.

Lawmakers probably won't let that happen. They may wait until the last minute to pass a fix, but they will most likely get it done. That's what happened in 1983, the last time Congress made major reforms to shore up Social Security. At that time, they waited until the eleventh hour to gradually raise the full retirement age to 67 from 65 and subject a portion of benefits to income taxes for the first time, among other changes.

Any changes this time around will likely spare current retirees and those approaching retirement. While younger Americans will probably see their future benefits reduced in some way, those who are within at least 10 years of retirement will most likely claim under the current benefit structure.

Most Americans understand that claiming Social Security early will reduce their monthly benefits for life. For those born in 1960 and later, claiming at your earliest eligibility of 62 will result in a monthly check that is 30% less than what it would be at 67, when you're entitled to 100% of your benefit. If you can hold out until 70, you'll get 124% of what you would have received at 67. The extra cash would be a welcome boost for the more than half of survey respondents who reported concerns about outliving their assets in retirement.

To be sure, there are good reasons to claim Social Security early. If you don't have other income and need the money to live on, then it doesn't make sense to wait. Ditto if you have a lower life expectancy due to a serious medical condition.

But if you can afford to wait, consider the various outcomes, says Ray R. Harris, founder of Social Security Claiming Experts: There's a 100% chance of a 30% benefit cut if you claim at 62, but a much smaller chance of Congress failing to act and a 22% benefit cut.
